summary: This experimental memo describes the Internet Relay Chat protocol, a text-based protocol for talking in channels with many people at once. It says the simplest client can be any program that opens a socket.

eli5.summary: IRC is an early chat system with rooms called channels. This paper explains the plain text messages that chat programs and servers use.

subtitle: The original text-based chat protocol: servers joined in a tree, clients with nicknames, and channels where many people talk at once.

tldr.problem: People wanted real-time text conferencing across many machines, not just one chat program on one host.
tldr.mechanism: Servers connect in a spanning tree over TCP. Clients connect to a server and exchange short text lines (commands such as NICK, JOIN and PRIVMSG), and the servers relay them along the tree to the right people and channels.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1459 describes the protocol as then implemented, including its known problems with scalability and name collisions. It is an Experimental memo and was later updated by several RFCs.

today: RFC 1459 is an Experimental memo, and it has been updated by RFC 2810, RFC 2811, RFC 2812, RFC 2813 and RFC 7194, so read those alongside it. The memo itself asks for discussion and improvement and points to the current IAB Official Protocol Standards for the standardization state.

sections.title: Servers, Clients and Channels
sections.content:
The IRC (Internet Relay Chat) protocol was designed over a number of years for text-based conferencing, and it was developed on systems using TCP/IP. The servers form the backbone: clients connect to a server, and other servers connect to it too, making up an IRC network. The only network layout allowed is a spanning tree, where each server acts as a central node for the part of the net it sees.

A client is anything connecting to a server that is not another server. Each client has a unique nickname of at most nine characters, and servers also know the client's host name, username and the server it is connected to. A special class of clients, operators, can do network maintenance such as disconnecting and reconnecting servers, and can forcibly remove a user with KILL. The RFC calls these powers dangerous but required.

A channel is a named group of clients that all receive messages sent to it. A channel is created implicitly when the first client joins and disappears when the last one leaves. Names start with a hash sign or an ampersand (such as #chat or &local), can be up to 200 characters, and cannot contain spaces, a control G or a comma. A hash-sign channel is known to all servers on the network, while an ampersand channel exists only on one server. The first user to join becomes the channel operator, and a limit of ten channels per user is recommended.
sections.eli5: Think of a school made of connected buildings. Each person has a nickname, and chat rooms exist only while someone is inside them. The person who opens a room is its boss.

sections.title: How a Message Looks
sections.content:
IRC is a text-based protocol, and the simplest client can be any program that opens a socket to the server. No specific character set is defined: messages are made of 8-bit octets, though the delimiters and keywords are such that the protocol is mostly usable from a US-ASCII terminal over telnet. Because of IRC's Scandinavian origin, the characters {}| count as the lower case forms of []\, which matters when comparing nicknames.

A message has up to three parts: an optional prefix, a command, and up to 15 parameters, all separated by spaces. A prefix starts with a colon and tells where the message really came from. The last parameter may start with a colon so that it can contain spaces. Each message ends with a carriage return and line feed, and messages must not exceed 512 characters including that CR-LF, which leaves 510 for the command and parameters. There is no way to continue a message on another line.

Most commands produce a reply. The usual form is a numeric reply, a three-digit code sent with the sender prefix and the target, used for both errors and normal answers. Clients are not allowed to originate numeric replies, and servers silently drop any they receive from a client. Communication is essentially asynchronous, so a client should not wait forever for a reply.
sections.eli5: Every message is one short line of text, like a text message with a limit on length. It can start with who it is from, then says what to do, and then gives the details.

sections.title: Connecting and Registering
sections.content:
A connection is registered as either a user or a server. For a client, the recommended order is PASS, then NICK, then USER. The password is optional for clients, but a server MUST send PASS before any SERVER command, and the RFC strongly recommends passwords on all server connections.

NICK gives or changes a nickname. If a server already knows the nickname for another client, a nickname collision occurs: all instances of the nickname are removed and a KILL removes it from other servers' databases. USER supplies username, host name, server name and real name, and a user becomes registered only after both USER and NICK have been received. Since a client can easily lie about its username, the RFC recommends an "Identity Server".

SERVER introduces a server, with a hop count and some info text. If it names a server that is already known, the connection must be closed because a duplicate route has broken the tree's acyclic shape. OPER lets a user obtain operator privileges with a name and password, and QUIT ends a session. SQUIT tells about a quitting or dead server, and when two servers are split, the quit message for affected users names the two servers involved.
sections.eli5: To join, you introduce yourself in order: say the secret password if there is one, pick a nickname, and tell the server who you are. If someone already has your nickname, the server kicks both of you out to avoid confusion.

sections.title: Joining Channels and Controlling Them
sections.content:
A user starts listening to a channel with JOIN. Only the server the client is connected to decides whether the join is allowed. The conditions are that the user must be invited if the channel is invite-only, must not match an active ban, and must give the correct key (password) if one is set. After a successful join the user is sent the channel topic and the list of users on it, and the JOIN is broadcast to all servers so each knows where channel members are.

PART leaves a channel. MODE changes the properties of a channel or a user. Channel modes include o (channel operator), p (private), s (secret), i (invite-only), t (only operators set the topic), n (no messages from outside), m (moderated), l (user limit), b (ban mask), v (voice on a moderated channel) and k (key). User modes are i, s, w and o.

Channel operators, shown by an @ next to their nickname, can use KICK, MODE, INVITE and TOPIC. The RFC says a channel operator is considered to own the channel and need not give reasons, although abuse can be reported to an IRC operator or users can leave and start their own channel.
sections.eli5: A room can be open, invite-only, password-protected or moderated. The room boss, marked with an @, can let people in, send them out, or change the rules.

sections.title: How Messages Travel
sections.content:
For one-to-one talk, a message travels the shortest path between two points on the spanning tree, and only the servers along that path see it. For example, in the RFC's Figure 2 a message between clients 2 and 4 is seen by servers A, B, C and D and by client 4 only.

The main goal of IRC is one-to-many conversation. Sending to a list of users is the least efficient way, because the server breaks the list up and sends a separate copy to each destination. A channel works like a multicast group: its membership changes dynamically and messages go only to servers that have members. If several users on one server are in a channel, the text goes to that server once and is then delivered to each of them.

Operators can also send to a host or server mask, using PRIVMSG with a #mask or $mask. The mask must contain at least one dot and no wildcard after the last dot, so a message cannot be broadcast to everyone by sending to #*. Most commands that change state, such as channel membership or modes, are sent to all servers by default, and nearly all server-originated messages are broadcast to all other servers.
sections.eli5: A private note only travels through the hallways between you and your friend. A message to a room is handed to each building once, and then that building passes copies to everyone inside.

sections.title: Implementation Notes and Known Problems
sections.content:
The only implementation then current was the IRC server version 2.8. It uses TCP, which the RFC says supplies a reliable network protocol suited to this scale of conferencing, and notes that multicast IP is an alternative but not widely available. Each connection has a 512-byte input buffer. Servers must ping connections that go quiet and close those that do not answer, and may also drop connections whose send queue grows beyond its maximum.

To protect the network from floods, servers penalize a client by 2 seconds for each message and parse messages only while the client's timer is less than ten seconds ahead, which in effect allows one message every 2 seconds. Servers must also keep a history of recent nickname changes to reduce race conditions for commands such as KILL and KICK.

The RFC lists its own problems. It does not scale well, because every server must know about all other servers, users and channels. Nicknames, channel names and server names can collide and lead to race conditions. There are no database consistency checks, so a buggy neighbouring server could introduce contradictions. The authors hoped to solve these in a rewrite. On security, the RFC only points to Sections 4.1, 4.1.1, 4.1.3, 5.5 and 7.
sections.eli5: The system works but has growing pains. Every building has to know about everyone, which gets hard as more people join, and two people picking the same nickname causes trouble.
